title: Request deserialization + tokenization overhead and thread scheduling probe
content:
Summary:

This note captures exploratory profiling and microbenchmarks focused on a recurring latency spike for small requests (<=64 tokens) that we've seen on a subset of serving hosts. Symptoms point to work being dominated by request deserialization + initial tokenization path on the CPU side, amplified by worker scheduling variability and occasional Python-side pauses (GC / interpreter transitions). This is an investigation log (not final), with reproducible harness notes, flamegraph excerpts (described), numbers, hypotheses, and short experiments to run next.

Context / why this matters:
- Tail latency on small requests matters disproportionately to product UX. Most samples are short and very latency sensitive.
- Prior work optimized the model-critical path (KV cache, decoding loops) but the pre-tokenization/parse stages haven't been systematically optimized.
- We need to decide whether to: 1) invest in C++/Rust preproc (moving tokenization/deser out of Python), 2) change scheduling/queue semantics (priority/affinity), or 3) tweak Python runtime knobs (GC tuning, subinterpreters, or GIL-escape strategies).

Observed symptom (production and local repro):
- p95 increases from ~60ms to ~160ms for small requests on ~15% of hosts during bursts. p99 sees larger jumps.
- Flamegraphs (sampled) show large slabs in: request parsing (json.loads), header sanitization, tokenizer.encode() and a non-trivial amount in "context switch / scheduler" (syscall entry/exit and pthread_cond_timedwait).
- Correlated spikes with CPU-stealing background jobs reported by node telemetry, but not all cases can be explained by host-level noise.

Test harness (how to reproduce deterministically):
1) Use small-req harness: 10k requests over 60 seconds, mean qps=170, payload size 200B, requests single-stream (no streaming).
2) Two worker configurations: a) async Python main thread with worker threadpool (current), b) hybrid: C++ preproc shim that does JSON parsing + simple tokenization (local std::string -> token ids) before handing to Python.
3) Collect perf samples (perf record -F 99 -g), and run py-spy sampling, and host vmstat/iostat to rule out IO noise.
4) Additionally run a microbench comparing json.loads vs orjson (v3.9) and our tokenizers: Python tokenizer v1 (pure-Python wrapper) vs quicknative v0.2 (Rust extension).

Microbench numbers (median of 10 runs, 64-bit host, 8 vCPU, pinned):
- json.loads (200B payload) median: 1.8 ms
- orjson.loads same payload median: 0.45 ms  (4x faster)
- tokenizer.py::encode (avg small prompt 40 chars) median: 2.7 ms
- quicknative tokenizer (Rust ext) median: 0.28 ms (10x faster)
- syscalls seen per request (current): ~8 (enter/exit Python C-API, gettimeofday, epoll_wait short poll)
- Python GC pause events observed as ~1-2ms spikes every ~600ms under existing heap churn (objects created by parser/tokenizer glue).

Key flamegraph observations (qualitative):
- "json.loads" and the Python tokenizer glue occupy ~35-45% of CPU on the slow samples; model inference kernel time is still dominant for long requests but negligible for short requests.
- There's a notable chain: socket recv -> parse headers -> json.loads -> call into tokenizer -> Python object allocation -> tokenizer loop. Between json.loads and tokenizer we see a few C->Python transitions that are not inlined by the profiler (overhead).
- Scheduling hotspots: several stacks end in pthread_cond_timedwait or epoll_wait where threads wake up and then immediately contend on a shared queue lock. Sampling indicates threads often spin briefly then block, indicating lock contention on worker queue head.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Deserialization and tokenizer overhead (pure-Python) are primary per-request CPU cost and dominate short-request p95.
2) Worker queue lock contention (coarse-grained lock around ready-queue) amplifies tail by introducing jitter between parse completion and model enqueuing.
3) Python GC and small-object churn from the tokenizer glue add a small but measurable periodic jitter.
4) Some hosts have background processes causing time-slice preemption, but that's a minority cause.

Experiments run so far and short results:
A) Swap json.loads -> orjson in request path (local canary): p95 reduced by ~22% on small-req harness. CPU profiles show deserialization slab shrunk considerably. No correctness issues seen.
B) Replace tokenizer call site with quicknative stub (Rust extension via cffi) that returns precomputed token ids for 95% of inputs (cache-like behavior): p95 reduced by ~40%-50% (very promising) but introduces complexity around building wheels for Private deployments.
C) Change worker queue lock from single mutex to MPSC per-worker queues with scheduler thread: eliminated short-lived contention in our harness, p95 improved ~15% further when combined with A/B. Slight increase in average memory for ring buffers.
D) Tweak Python GC thresholds (increase threshold 2x): reduced GC pause counts but net p95 improvement only ~3% -- GC was not the main lever.

Tradeoffs / operational considerations:
- Moving deserialization/tokenization out of Python (native extension or separate preproc service) gives best perf, but increases packaging/deployment complexity (wheel compatibility, private/on-prem). Also increases TCB surface (native code bugs).
- Using orjson is low-friction and large win; should be safe and is backwards-compatible in most cases. Patch-size small.
- Per-worker queues reduce lock contention but require changes to metrics collection and tracing (need to ensure request IDs propagate correctly across queues).

Quick wins recommended (short runway):
1) Immediate: Replace json.loads with orjson for request path and remove any redundant header reparsing. Roll a canary against low-traffic Dedicated cluster.
2) Short term (2–4 weeks): Introduce a vendored Rust tokenizer extension as an opt-in experiment behind a config flag; collect telemetry and fall back to Python if unavailable.
3) Mid term: Switch to per-worker queues + lightweight scheduler to reduce enqueuing jitter; ship with observability hooks to prove end-to-end latency improvement.

Longer-term options to evaluate (cost vs benefit):
- Split pre-processing into a small C++/Rust sidecar process that performs header parse + tokenization; communicates tokens over a compact binary wire to main runtime (zero-copy). Will reduce Python runtime dependency, but requires IPC and additional process lifecycle complexity.
- Investigate subinterpreters for true GIL escape for tokenizers (experimental, CPython v3.13+); pros/cons TBD.
- Rework API: accept token ids directly for internal customers to skip preproc (already exists but usage low). Consider multi-tenant tokenization cache layer.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Are there any compatibility concerns with orjson on older customers (edge cases in float parsing / decimals)? Need to audit tests.
- Can we vendor quicknative tokenizer in a way that satisfies Private deployment compliance (no native build step)? Build static wheels for common Linux ABIs?
- What's the engineering estimate to implement per-worker queues across our runtime (~2 sprints?) — need SRE signoff on memory overhead.

Next concrete actions (owners):
- Aisha: prepare canary patch swapping to orjson; run 72h canary and collect p50/p95/p99 and CPU flamegraphs. (ETA 4 days)
- Miguel: prototype per-worker queue scheduler and add low-overhead request-id propagation. (ETA 2 weeks)
- Priya: evaluate quicknative packaging story for Private (wheel matrix), and list minimal compliance checklist. (ETA 1 week)

Appendix: quick repro commands
- Harness runner (pseudo): python tools/harness/small_req.py --qps 170 --duration 60 --payload sample_small.json
- Perf sample: perf record -F 99 -g -- python -m gunicorn --config ...
- py-spy: py-spy record -o flame.svg -- python -m serving.runtime --config ...

Notes to self: keep this doc as the working log; move final recommendations into product PRD once canary validates orjson. Save heavy instrumentation (eBPF) for next milestone if variance unexplained after native tokenizer + scheduling changes.

-- Aisha
